## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vaṇṇārohajātaka* (Ja 361) is a narrative birth story preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Pali Canon. The verse text opens with the incipit *Vaṇṇārohena* [Fausböll 1883]. According to the canonical frame narrative, the Buddha delivered this teaching while residing at Jetavana in connection with his two chief disciples, Sāriputta and Moggallāna [Fausböll 1883]. In the introductory account (*paccuppannavatthu*), the two chief disciples take leave of the Teacher to spend their rains retreat (*antovassa*) in the solitude of the wilderness near a border village [Fausböll 1883]. André Migot discusses this Jātaka in his study of Sāriputta, highlighting it as an example of the legendary harmony and friendship between Sāriputta and Moggallāna, which an outsider unsuccessfully sought to undermine [Migot, Śāriputra]. In the conclusion and identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the treacherous jackal (*sigāla*) is identified as an offal-eater (*vighāsāda*), the lion as Sāriputta, the tiger as Moggallāna, and the observing forest tree-deity (*vanadevatā*) as the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1883].

 Computationally, DharmaNexus identifies significant textual overlap and reuse with the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also registers low-scoring automated cross-language alignments with Tibetan canonical collections and the *Mahāvyutpatti* (D4346) [DharmaNexus]. The text was edited by V. Fausböll in his critical edition of the Jātaka with commentary [Fausböll 1883], and is referenced in Anandajoti's collection of canonical verses [Anandajoti 2010].
